Who I work with

You might be here because…

01

You love each other, but feel worlds apart

Different cultural backgrounds, different families, different expectations about how love is supposed to work. The gap feels real — and exhausting.

02

You need a therapist who won't make you explain yourselves

You're tired of educating the room about your identity, your culture, or your relationship structure. You want someone who just gets it.

03

Something has broken trust

An affair, a betrayal, a slow erosion. You're not sure what you want — to stay, to leave, or just to understand what happened.

04

You're not in crisis — you just want to do better

The relationship is good, but you sense it could be more. Deeper. More honest. You're investing before things break down.

About Jessie

I know what it's like
to live between worlds.

I grew up between cultures — my parents immigrated across countries, and I've since lived in the US, China, Sweden, and the UK, with time in Italy, Hong Kong, and Ghana. My partner is from a different cultural background and was also adopted. I navigate this complexity in my own life, not just in the consulting room.

Before private practice I worked with domestic violence organisations, Asian American community groups, immigration shelters, and refugee populations — because the world outside a relationship doesn't stay outside. It comes into the room.

How I work

Evidence-based approaches,
chosen for fit — not fashion

No single model works for every couple. I draw on several evidence-based frameworks, combining them based on what the relationship needs — not what fits a template.

EFT

Emotionally Focused Therapy

Works at the level of attachment — the emotional bond between partners, and the cycles of pursuit and withdrawal that form when that bond feels threatened. The strongest evidence base of any couples model.

Gottman Method

Gottman Method

Research-based tools for building friendship, managing conflict, and creating shared meaning — developed from 40 years of research on what makes relationships succeed or fail.

Systemic

Systemic & Psychodynamic

Looks at the wider systems — families, cultures, histories — that both partners bring into the room. Essential for intercultural couples, where context is never just background.

Areas of specialism

Where I do my deepest work

Intercultural & Interracial Couples

When two people come from different cultural backgrounds, the relationship carries two sets of assumptions about family, love, conflict, and loyalty — often unspoken, often invisible until they clash.

  • Cultural differences in communication and conflict
  • Family pressure and loyalty conflicts
  • Bicultural identity and belonging
  • Immigration and acculturative stress
  • Raising children between cultures
  • Adoption and complex family-of-origin stories

LGBTQ+ Affirming Couples Therapy

LGBTQ+ couples face pressures that heteronormative therapy simply isn't built to see — minority stress, chosen family dynamics, relationships that don't fit received templates.

  • Minority stress and its relational impact
  • Coming out and family estrangement
  • Non-traditional relationship structures
  • Identity and transition within a partnership
  • The intersection of LGBTQ+ and intercultural identity
  • Navigating visibility and safety as a couple

My parents left everything they knew. I grew up in the space that created.

My parents immigrated across countries — and I grew up between the world they came from and the world I was born into. That gap, the one between where you're from and where you are, between what your family taught you love looks like and what your partner expects it to mean — is something I have navigated my entire life.

I've lived in the United States, China, Sweden, and the United Kingdom, with significant time in Italy, Hong Kong, and Ghana. Each place taught me something different about what relationships are supposed to look like — what's said, what's silenced, what counts as intimacy, what counts as respect. I learned that none of those things are universal, even when they feel like they are.

My partner is from a different culture and background than mine, and was also adopted — which adds another layer of complexity to questions about family, belonging, and where you come from. I'm not working from theory alone. I understand these dynamics because I live inside them.

Before private practice

Where I learned that everything
lives inside the relationship

🏠

Domestic Violence Organisations

Working with couples and individuals affected by domestic violence showed me the extremes of what power imbalance does to intimacy — and gave me a precise, unsentimental understanding of how control operates in close relationships.

🌸

Asian American Community Organisations

This work deepened my understanding of the specific pressures that fall on couples navigating between family cultures and Western social norms — the weight of expectation, the cost of difference, the particular silences that form between generations and between partners.

✈️

Immigration Shelters

Migration reshapes people in ways that ripple into every close relationship they have. Working in immigration shelters taught me about the particular grief of losing your context — and about the extraordinary resourcefulness of people building new lives under profound uncertainty.

🌍

Refugee Population Support

Relationships under displacement survive things most couples can barely imagine. This work gave me a profound respect for resilience, and a clinical understanding of how trauma changes what intimacy means and how safety has to be rebuilt.

This isn't background colour. The people I worked with in these settings are the reason I understand that a relationship doesn't exist in isolation — that racism, displacement, poverty, and structural pressure don't stay outside the door when a couple sits down to talk.

"I understand this terrain because I live inside it."

What I believe

The principles that
guide this work

01

Context is not optional

You cannot understand a relationship without understanding the worlds that formed each person in it. Culture, history, family systems, and social pressures are not background detail — they're structure.

02

Difference is not damage

Being different from your partner is not a problem to fix. It's a reality to work with — and when worked with well, it can be a source of extraordinary depth and connection.

03

Both people are always in the room

I don't take sides. My client is the relationship — and both people deserve to feel heard, understood, and not managed. That requires active, genuine neutrality.

04

Insight without change is just biography

Understanding why a pattern exists matters. But the goal is something shifting — in how you reach for each other, how you repair, how you build something neither of you has had before.

05

Lived experience matters in the therapist too

I bring my own navigation of cultural complexity into the room — not as oversharing, but as genuine understanding. Clients shouldn't have to explain what it means to be between worlds.

06

The relationship is worth the work

People come to therapy when they still believe something is possible. That belief — even when fragile — is always somewhere in the room. My job is to help them find it again.

My approach

Therapy that goes
deep enough
to actually move.

A lot of couples have talked. What they haven't done is talk in a way that reaches the thing underneath the argument — the fear, the need, the unspoken story. That's what the work is for.

The questions couples bring — and what I actually do with them

Most couples arrive with a presenting problem: "we keep having the same fight," "we've lost intimacy," "I don't know if I still love them." These are real, and they matter. But the presenting problem is rarely the whole story.

What's underneath it — the patterns, the attachment fears, the cultural framings of what love is supposed to look like — is where the actual work lives. My job is to create a space where both partners can begin to see that layer, and to shift within it.

[ Add 2–3 sentences here about your personal philosophy of change — what do you believe has to happen for something to shift? ]

Will you take sides?

No. My client is the relationship — not either individual. Both of you need to feel genuinely heard, not managed. I work hard to maintain active, real neutrality — not just a claim to it.

Do I have to explain my culture or identity?

No. I work with intercultural and LGBTQ+ couples because I understand those dynamics from the inside, not just the literature. You won't spend session time educating me.

How long does therapy take?

There's no fixed programme. Some couples need 8–10 sessions to address a specific issue. Others work with me for a year or more. We check in regularly on what's useful and when it makes sense to stop.

Do both partners need to come?

For couples therapy, yes — both partners attend together. Occasionally I may suggest brief individual sessions as part of the work, but the core sessions are joint.

Is there homework?

Sometimes. Depending on what we're working on, I may suggest things to try between sessions. Nothing arbitrary — always connected to the work.

What if we're considering separation?

You don't need to have decided anything to start. Some couples come still invested; others are genuinely unsure. Both are valid starting points. Therapy can help with the decision as much as with the repair.

The methods I use

Evidence-based approaches,
chosen for fit — not fashion

No single model works for every couple. I draw on several evidence-based frameworks, combining them based on what I'm seeing in the room — the couple's attachment patterns, cultural context, the nature of the conflict, and what stage of the work we're in.

EFT
Emotionally Focused Therapy

What it does

EFT works at the level of attachment — the deep emotional bond between partners, and the cycles of pursuit and withdrawal that form when that bond feels threatened. The goal is to shift how partners reach for each other.

Why I use it

EFT has the strongest evidence base of any couples therapy model. Particularly powerful for intercultural couples, where the attachment cycle is often complicated by different cultural scripts for vulnerability.

GM
Gottman Method

What it does

Developed from 40 years of research, the Gottman Method provides concrete tools for managing conflict, building friendship and intimacy, and creating shared meaning. Particularly good at naming specific patterns couples can recognise in their own dynamic.

Why I use it

Some couples need insight but also something more concrete. Gottman provides that. It also has specific research on same-sex couples, making it more applicable to LGBTQ+ partnerships than models developed on heterosexual samples only.

SFT
Systemic & Family Systems

What it does

Looks at the relationship not just between two individuals, but between those individuals and the larger systems around them — families of origin, cultures, communities, structural pressures. Asks: what is this pattern a response to?

Why I use it

This is where intercultural and LGBTQ+ work particularly needs a systemic lens. A couple's conflict about money or family almost always has a cultural story inside it. Systemic work makes that visible without pathologising either partner.

PD
Psychodynamic

What it does

Looks at the deeper patterns — the relational templates formed in early life, the unconscious processes that play out between partners, the ways that past relationships shape present ones. Asks what each person is re-enacting.

Why I use it

Some couples are stuck in patterns that have nothing to do with each other and everything to do with what they each brought into the relationship. For couples where early experience of loss or instability is clearly present, this lens is often essential.

In the room

What a session actually looks like

I don't run sessions off a script. But there's a structure to how I work, and it's worth knowing what to expect — especially if you've never been to couples therapy before.

Sessions are 75 minutes for an initial assessment and 60 minutes for ongoing work. Both partners are in the room throughout. I tend to work with what's live — what's happening between you in the session, not just what you report from the week.

[ Add a sentence or two about your style — are you quieter and observational? More directive? Do you name patterns as you see them? ]

I work in-person in London and online. Both are effective — the research on online couples therapy is genuinely positive.

What this isn't

Worth being honest about

✕

I won't referee

I'm not here to decide who's right. If that's what you're looking for, this probably isn't the right fit. What I can do is help both of you understand why you're each so sure you're right.

✕

I won't pretend culture doesn't matter

Some therapists treat cultural difference as neutral background. I don't. If how you were each taught to express love or handle conflict is part of what's creating friction — we're going to talk about it.

✕

I won't use therapy as a performance space

Some couples use sessions to perform for the therapist. I'll gently redirect when that's happening, because the work happens when something real is being said.

✕

I won't push you toward a particular outcome

Whether you stay together or separate is not something I have a view on. Both can be the right outcome. Therapy is for understanding — not for reaching a conclusion I've already decided on.

Specialism one

Intercultural &
Interracial Couples

When two people come from different cultural worlds, the relationship carries more than just two individuals. It carries two complete sets of assumptions about what love, family, and loyalty are supposed to mean.

Specialism two

LGBTQ+
Affirming Therapy

LGBTQ+ couples face pressures that heteronormative therapy simply isn't built to see. You shouldn't have to explain yourselves to your therapist before the real work can begin.

01Specialism

Intercultural &
Interracial Couples

When two people come from different cultural backgrounds, the relationship isn't just between two individuals. It's between two complete sets of assumptions about how the world works and how love is supposed to feel.

The argument isn't really about whether you call her mother this weekend. It's about whether family loyalty means the same thing to both of you. The silence isn't about being tired. It's about what each of you learned it means to be emotionally close.

I bring to this work something beyond training: lived experience. I grew up between cultures, have lived across four continents, and am in an intercultural relationship myself — one that includes the additional complexity of adoption and different family-of-origin stories.

Cultural scripts for love and conflict

Every culture teaches its children a different script for expressing love, managing disagreement, and showing vulnerability. When two scripts collide, the result is often conflict that neither partner fully understands — because it's happening below the level of the words.

Family involvement and loyalty conflicts

In individualist cultures, the couple is the primary unit. In collectivist ones, the family is. When partners come from different sides of this divide, questions about parents, in-laws, and money become proxy battles for much deeper differences about what marriage actually means.

Bicultural identity and belonging

Many people in intercultural relationships are also navigating their own bicultural identity — the experience of belonging fully to neither culture. This has specific relational effects: the fear of assimilation, the grief of distance from origin.

Unequal external pressure

When one partner belongs to a dominant culture and the other doesn't, the relationship carries a power differential that most couples don't name. Racism, microaggressions, family disapproval — these come into the relationship and need to be addressed there.

Raising children between cultures

Questions of language, religion, naming, schooling, and cultural transmission become live and often fraught. Therapy can help couples develop a shared framework — not a compromise, but something genuinely co-created.

Adoption and complex family-of-origin stories

When one or both partners were adopted, or have limited knowledge of their heritage, it changes questions about belonging and identity. Standard assessment tools often don't fit. I work differently when this is part of the picture.

📖

What the research says: A 2024 scoping review found that despite the growing prevalence of intercultural relationships, there remains a significant paucity of empirical evidence on how cultural differences should be addressed in therapy — and a particular gap around the intersection of intercultural and LGBTQ+ identities. Working with a therapist who has both specialist training and lived experience in this area makes a meaningful clinical difference.

Yurtaeva & Charura, Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 2024 · Su, Personal Relationships, 2023
02Specialism

LGBTQ+
Affirming
Couples Therapy

LGBTQ+ couples face pressures that most mainstream couples therapy models weren't built to address — not because they're more fragile, but because they're navigating a set of conditions that heterosexual, cisgender couples simply don't encounter.

Minority stress is real and it lives in the relationship. The chronic experience of discrimination, concealment, family rejection, and navigating an often-hostile world has direct effects on how partners attach to each other and what safety in intimacy feels like.

I work within an explicitly affirming framework — I won't ask you to justify your relationship structure, won't treat your identity as a variable to be bracketed, and won't default to heteronormative assumptions.

Minority stress and its relational effects

Chronic exposure to stigma and discrimination changes how people attach and express need. In couples, this often shows up as difficulty with vulnerability, hypervigilance to rejection, or conflict patterns that make more sense when minority stress is understood as a driver.

Coming out, family estrangement, chosen family

The relational consequences of coming out — family loss, chosen family dynamics, ongoing decisions about disclosure — create a specific context for LGBTQ+ couples that heterosexual couples don't navigate.

Non-traditional relationship structures

LGBTQ+ couples are more likely to have relationship structures that don't fit the templates couples therapy was built around. I work from the assumption that your structure is valid; the question is how to make it work well for you.

Identity transitions within a partnership

When one partner transitions — in gender, sexual identity, or relationship to their LGBTQ+ identity — both partners may need to renegotiate who they are to each other and what the relationship means.

The intersection of LGBTQ+ and intercultural identity

When a couple is both LGBTQ+ and intercultural, the complexity multiplies. This is one of the least-researched areas in couples therapy, and one I have particular experience with.

Navigating visibility and safety as a couple

Being out as a couple — in different contexts, around different family members — involves constant negotiation. When partners have different levels of outness or different risk tolerances, this becomes a live tension in the relationship.

Worth being clear

Who this is and isn't for

Specialising in intercultural and LGBTQ+ work doesn't mean I only work with couples who fit those categories. It means I'm equipped to hold that complexity when it's present, without making clients educate me first.

This isn't identity-focused therapy for every session

Many sessions are about communication, trust, intimacy — the same things any couple works on. The specialism means I understand the context. It doesn't mean every conversation is about race or sexuality.

You don't have to be in "crisis"

Some couples I work with are in real distress. Others are doing reasonably well and want to go deeper — to build something more intentional before difficulty arrives. Both are valid reasons to start.

I also work with couples outside these categories

If you're drawn to the approach — the depth, the cultural attentiveness, the willingness to go underneath the presenting problem — that's worth a conversation.
